1:
Keil and Delitzsch set the section against the impending fall of the kingdom of Judah, where the prophet seeks to give the godly a strong anchor of hope in promises to be fulfilled after the appointed season of punishment has passed; following Hengstenberg they call the address the triumphal hymn of Israel salvation. Calvin reads the opening as a deliberate preface. The people were so possessed by stupor that Jeremiah had been addressing the deaf, or rather stocks and stones, and God prefixes these words that they might be the more attentive to what follows. Gill notes only that the word of prophecy came, as the Targum renders it, and that Kimchi observes it to be a consolatory one.

The command to write draws the sharpest comment. Henry has it written not in a letter, as the message to the captives had been, but in a book to be kept among the public rolls or registers of the state, so that those who did not profit by hearing might take more notice on a considered review, and that generations to come might see it accomplished and have their faith confirmed; he observes that Daniel understood from these books when the captivity was drawing to an end. Clarke fixes the extent of the book narrowly, since among the Hebrews any portion of writing in which the subject was finished, however small, was termed a book. Ellicott reaches the same extent with less confidence: there is no definite point at which we may be certain the section ends, and there is room for conjecture about interpolations, but the opening of a later chapter suggests it takes in the whole of both. He alone presses what the writing itself signifies, that what follows was not spoken first in the presence of the people, as earlier oracles had been, but was from the first committed to writing.

The voices divide over when the promised return falls. Clarke gives two moments, after the conclusion of the seventy years and under the Messiah, and reports that Dahler dated the prophecy about a year after the taking of Jerusalem while Blayney referred it to the times of the Gospel, touching also at the restoration at the end of seventy years. His own judgment is stronger: no deliverance hitherto afforded comes up to the terms of it, since after the return the people were enslaved by the Greeks and Romans, so the prophecy remains to be fulfilled in the reign of David, the type being put for the antitype. Gill cites Kimchi for the days of the Messiah but denies the first coming, referring it instead to a spiritual coming in the latter day.

On scope, Clarke reads Israel as the ten tribes led captive by the king of Assyria and dispersed among the nations, and Judah as those carried to Babylon under Jeconiah and then under Zedekiah by Nebuchadnezzar. Ellicott hears an earlier oracle becoming the text of a new utterance with a wider range, including the ten tribes as well as Judah and Benjamin, the prophet yearning for exiles on the Euphrates and for those yet farther off in Assyria and the cities of the Medes. Calvin agrees on the order, the ten tribes named first because their exile was much longer, and returns to his controlling contrast: the false prophets had fed the people with the hope of a return after two years, and when that time had passed every expectation failed, so that the prophet must recall them to quietness of mind and teach them that God would prove faithful.
4:
Calvin opens with a protest. Both Jews and Christians pervert the passage, he says, by applying it to the time of the Messiah, and they are wonderfully united here where they hardly agree as to any other part of Scripture; whoever views the whole context wisely will see instead that the prophet includes the sum of the doctrine the people had previously heard from his mouth. The first clause touches on the vengeance resting on the people, but only briefly, since the object was chiefly to alleviate the sorrow of the afflicted, and the reason for the command to write was to supply the exiles with comfort after God had destroyed the Temple and the city. Gill passes the verse over in a line.

The cry of trembling raises the question of whose voice it is. Gill observes that what follows are the words of others, and reports Kimchi and Ben Melech taking them as what the Gentiles will say in the times of the Messiah, though he would rather supply the words as spoken by Israel and Judah themselves. Calvin has God speak in the person of the people in order to expose their insensibility. They were not terrified by threatenings, however many and dreadful, so God dictated words for them; and though they deride and scoff, or remain insensible in their delusions as the drunken, God will yet extort from them this voice of trembling and fear. Clarke takes the terror historically, referring it to the state and feelings of the people during the war which Cyrus carried on against the Babylonians, when they could not tell whether their own condition would be better or worse should their present masters fall in the conflict.

On the man in travail, Gill would have the reader look into the histories of former times and inquire of those most versed in them whether there was ever such a thing in the world. Calvin insists that the monstrosity is the whole point: it is natural for a man to beget, so the prophet asks ironically whether a man can be in labour, because God would put all men into pains and agonies not manly, their hands laid on their loins like a woman when her pain is greatest and most bitter. He was vehement here, Calvin adds, because a common mode of speaking would not have moved a people so perverse. Clarke identifies the great day with the coming of the Medes and Persians upon the Chaldeans, and finds the deliverance doubled: the Jews were delivered by Cyrus when that empire fell, and when Jerusalem was destroyed by the Romans not one who had embraced Christianity perished in the ruin of the city.

The yoke is identified with one voice. Clarke and Wesley both make it the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar, the power he exercised over the Jews for seventy years, and read the one whose service ends as the captive Jews themselves. Calvin agrees and supplies the timing: the false prophets inflamed the people with the expectation of a deliverance after two years, but God had assigned a day, the seventieth year, and bade the faithful wait rather than be in a hurry; deliverance is promised only to those who suffer themselves to be paternally chastised, since to resist when goaded is wilfully to provoke God. Ellicott notes how strangely the second and third person are mingled, Jehovah speaking to Israel of thy bonds and thy yoke while the yoke of him is the oppressor, and hears the prophet echoing the words of Isaiah. Keil and Delitzsch carry the promise forward: Israel will no longer serve strangers, foreign rulers who are heathens, but their God and David the king whom he will raise up to them.
9:
David their king divides the voices. Clarke refers it necessarily to the times of the Messiah, and calls in the Chaldee, which renders it that they shall obey the Messiah the Son of David: a very remarkable version, he says, made not according to the letter but according to their own doctrine and expectation. His argument is historical. David was long since dead, none of his descendants reigned after the captivity, and neither Zerubbabel under the Persians nor the Asmoneans is an exception; they have been no nation since and are none now. Ellicott takes the name as that of the new representative of the house, a second David answering to the ideal which the old hero-king imperfectly represented, and allows that Zerubbabel was in his measure another partial representative. Wesley leaves the alternative open: either the kingdom of Christ, under which the Jews who received him were made spiritually free, or a civil liberty yet to come. Gill reads the service as spiritual, in righteousness and true holiness.

Calvin makes the clause structural rather than messianic. The former promise would have been defective without it, since it would not be enough for men to live as they please and have liberty promised them unless a regular order were established; better to be wild beasts wandering in forests, he says, than to live without government and laws, knowing how furious the passions of men are. The verse is added that the people might know nothing would be wanting to them: having served strangers they would now be under the government of God and of their own king, and that subjection is better than all the ruling powers of the world.

On the exhortation not to fear, Calvin observes that assurance of divine goodwill is not enough by itself, since experience teaches how backward and slow we are to embrace the promises, and our listlessness renders many goads necessary. He weighs the two verbs: the second is stronger than fear, meaning to be broken down in mind so as to give up all hope, and the two answer to two grounds of dread, a final return and the distance from which it must come, the order as commonly reversed. Ellicott hears the higher strain in the parallelism of the clauses, calls the whole verse poetic in form, and catches something of the ring of Isaiah, whose language Gill hears too. Keil and Delitzsch identify the servant as the true Israel, faithful and devoted to God, who shall dwell in peace and undisturbed security in their own land.

The measured correction is the note all take. Henry sets God himself against them as the principal agent whoever the instruments were, yet insists the chastisement is fatherly and no more than deserved or than can well be borne, and warns that a profession of religion however plausible secures no impunity, since God shows his hatred of sin most in those nearest him. Wesley reads in measure as moderation and not equity only. Ellicott draws the contrast furthest: the destruction of the heathen nations was to be complete and irreversible, so that Moab and Ammon and Edom should no more have a place in the history of the world, while the punishment of Israel was remedial as well as retributive, and to be left altogether unpunished would be the most terrible of all punishments. Calvin explains why the comparison was needed, since the Chaldeans and the Assyrians flourished seventy years in every kind of wealth while the people were counted as sheep destined for the slaughter. Clarke states it plainly: though the Persians destroy the nations they vanquish, they shall not destroy thee.
12:
The word rendered incurable is contested at once. Clarke corrects it: the term means desperate, not incurable, since the cure is promised a few verses on, where health is restored and the wounds healed. Calvin takes it as a substantive followed by a preposition, so the sentence must run that grievousness is to thy bruising, and the wound is difficult to be healed rather than past healing. Ellicott hears the prophet dwelling on the seeming hopelessness in words that sound like an echo of his own Lamentations, and says he does it to enhance the blessedness of the hope that follows. Gill alone presses the despair forward, finding no help from men and no likelihood of recovery to the former state and glory, so that whenever restoration comes it will be as life from the dead, like quickening the dry bones of Ezekiel.

Calvin keeps his eye on the controversy behind the passage. The prophet was fighting with the impostors who gave the people hope of a return in a short time when seventy years were to be expected, and he dwelt at length on the grievousness of the evils not because the people were insensible but because they had been credulous, deceiving themselves with false comfort. Nothing, Calvin says, is more difficult than to lead men to a serious acknowledgment of judgment, since they are tender and sensitive as to the evils they endure and yet do not look to God. Wesley states the ground more bluntly, that they had sinned to such a degree that captivity was resolved on. Henry turns it into a question with its own answer, that when God is against a people none can be for them so as to do them any kindness, and adds that incurable griefs are owing to incurable lusts, and that every effort to heal ourselves proves fruitless so long as we neglect the heavenly Advocate and the sanctifying Spirit.

The want of an advocate draws out the imagery. Ellicott finds two images of extremest misery pressed together, the criminal standing before the dread judgment-seat with no advocate and the plague-stricken sufferer with no physician, and repunctuates the second clause to read that there are no healing medicines for binding up. Gill has nobody willing to take the trouble to look into the wound, to judge of it and debate what methods are advisable, or to compress it so as to squeeze out the corrupt matter. Calvin notes that the prophet speaks first without a figure and then illustrates the simple truth by a metaphor, and that he includes in one sentence the whole first chapter of Isaiah. Wesley reduces the lesson to its practical point: there was no present remedy but patience, whatever cure the false prophets might promise. Keil and Delitzsch look past it to the reversal, where the enemies who would devour Israel meet the fate they had prepared for Zion.

The lovers are named without dispute. Gill and Wesley alike identify them as the Egyptians and Assyrians, sought for help and bound by alliance, who promised great things and then forgot their promises. Calvin rejects the gentler reading that friends merely concealed themselves through shame at a hopeless case, and makes the verse a condemnation of the false confidence that had long fascinated the people: such confederacies are compared throughout the prophets to impure lusts, so that to seek at one time the friendship of the Egyptians and at another that of the Assyrians was a kind of adultery in a people God had taken under his own care. Ellicott takes the lovers for allies and tributaries, naming Moab, Ammon, Edom and Tyre as having once courted the favour of Judah and now looking on her as smitten of God and afflicted.
15:
Calvin reads the question as an anticipated objection. The people always complained of extreme severity while indulging their vices, and grew exasperated as soon as God treated them as they deserved; so the prophet meets their perverse and unjust complaints by deriding their late crying, which comes long after the season for repentance had passed. Gill puts it more shortly: when men have sinned at a high rate they have no reason to complain of the punishment of their sins. Ellicott keeps the personification running, looking on Judah as on some forlorn and desperate castaway smitten with pestilence and crying in the agony of her hopelessness, and finds hope precisely in her accepting the law of retribution, since her oppressors would come under that same law and the wheel would come full circle. Clarke only repeats his correction, that the word means desperate.

The reversal is read at different depths. Clarke traces a chain of empires: the Assyrians were destroyed by the Babylonians, the Babylonians by the Medes and Persians, the Egyptians and Persians by the Greeks under Alexander, and all these nations are now extinct while the Jews as a distinct people still exist. Gill carries it further than the destruction of the Babylonish empire by the Persians, to the Romans who ate up their substance and were themselves devoured by the Goths and Vandals, and notes that Jarchi calls the promise an oath. He weighs the connective too, preferring notwithstanding to therefore, so that the sense is that though they had sinned at so great a rate their enemies should still not go unpunished. Keil and Delitzsch simply head what follows as a further explanation of the deliverance promised to Zion.

The healing promise gives Calvin his most useful distinction. Unprincipled men who basely pretend the name of God have this in common with his true and faithful servants, that both hold forth his favour; but those who falsely use the name bury the doctrine of repentance, seeking only to soothe the people with flatteries and omitting whatever might offend and is in no way pleasant to the flesh. They boasted that God was merciful, slow to wrath and ready to be reconciled to sinners, and concluded from it that the exile would not be long. Jeremiah too gave hope of pardon and mitigated the severity of his doctrine, but he did not by indulgence cherish the vices of the people.

On the cure itself, Ellicott renders the promise literally as the placing of a healing plaster and resumes the image of the plague-stricken sufferer: men had scorned her and flung the contemptuous term of outcast at her, she was like Tyre, a harlot that had been forgotten, and no nation courted her alliance, so that the extremest misery seemed to touch the heart of Jehovah with pity even for the adulteress who had forsaken him, and the whole passage brings the parable of Gomer vividly to mind. Gill offers alternatives for the same phrase, that God will cause length to ascend, a long plaster, or prosperity long looked for and long in coming, or that a people bowed down with afflictions should now stand erect in their full height. Calvin makes the logic turn on who wounded them: he who inflicts wounds can alone heal, and having exercised judgment in punishing he afterwards undertakes the office of a Physician. The people had nearly rotted in their exile before deliverance came, and might a hundred times have been overwhelmed with despair, but they are bidden to raise their minds upward and expect help from heaven, for there was none on earth.
18:
The promise takes a material form, and the voices fill it in. Gill reads the tents of Jacob as the captives of Israel themselves, alluding to the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob dwelling in tents and to the Israelites in the wilderness, and finds the figure fitting for the present unsettled state of the people. Ellicott sees the tents of those who still kept up the old nomadic life pitched once more in the land, while for those who dwell in towns city and palace rise again from their ruins upon their old foundations in the hills of Judah. Clarke distinguishes the tents from the dwelling-places, understanding by them all the minor dispersions as well as the numerous synagogues found in large cities. Henry presses the reversal: the situation of Jerusalem was unexceptionable, so it shall be rebuilt upon the same spot, and he who can make of a city a heap can when he pleases make of a heap a city again.

The palace is read two ways. Clarke allows that the house of the king may be meant but thinks it more probably the temple, which was in fact rebuilt after the captivity, and points to the book of Nehemiah. Henry takes it as the temple outright, built after the old model with the service constantly kept up as formerly. Calvin does not press the buildings at all, dwelling instead on the speaker: God is introduced as though already prepared with an outstretched hand, because the people thought themselves wholly forsaken, and the cause named for their redemption is mercy alone, so that they might learn to flee to their only asylum.

On the thanksgiving, Calvin contrasts the sighings and lamentations of exile, when no praise could have been heard among them, with the full mouth by which God is blessed when some cause of joy is presented; sorrow is no hindrance to blessing God in extreme misery, he grants, citing the saying of James that the joyful should sing. He hears an indirect exhortation in the words, since the faithful are reminded to what end God deals so kindly with them, that they may proclaim his goodness. Henry makes the same point more compactly, that the voice of thanksgiving is the same with the voice of those that make merry, for whatever is the matter of our joy should be the matter of our praise. Gill adds that the sacrifices will not be the ceremonial ones, now seen to be abolished, but praise and thanksgiving only.

The children as aforetime divide them. Gill reports the opinion that the words look back to the patriarchs before the law was given, so that the law being abrogated they shall live without it as their forefathers did, and himself allows a spiritual sense of the children of the church born again as formerly. Calvin will not have this refinement, doubting that such a notion ever entered the mind of the prophet, and refers the words instead to the kingdom of David, the state of the church being no less prosperous under Christ than it was then. He justifies the abundance of words as necessary, since no token of favour appeared for seventy years and we are prone to despond, so that promises must be joined to promises, and if one will not suffice another may. Clarke has them educating their own children as formerly, with their religious assemblies established. Keil and Delitzsch take the parallel clauses about the prince and the ruler to mean that the people will no longer be subdued by foreign masters but ruled by leaders drawn out of their own midst and endowed with princely glory, in which is contained the truth that the restored sovereignty culminates in the kingdom of the Messiah.
21:
The clause about the nobles is read as singular or plural, and everything follows from that. Clarke keeps it plain and historical: strangers shall not rule over them, and both Nehemiah and Zerubbabel, their nobles and governors after the return from Babylon, were of their own people. Gill takes the word as one noble One, the noble One of Jacob, the Messiah in whom all the promises centre and whose incarnation and priesthood are the foundation of everything predicted here, and notes that the Targum interprets the words of him. Ellicott agrees on the number, rendering it literally as his glorious one and pointing to some single ruler, the word being the same as the excellent of one of the psalms.

Ellicott presses the question that follows further than the rest. It points, he says, to the ruler of the house of David whom the prophet sees in vision, in other words to the far-off Messiah, and he compares the like introduction of a conqueror in Isaiah who is asked who this is that comes from Edom. The dominant thought is of one who will not be treacherous or faithless, like the degenerate heirs of the house of David whom Jeremiah had known, but who would engage, or pledge and give as security, his heart and soul to the service of Jehovah. In the words about approaching, Ellicott finds the germ of a further thought, that the true king will also be a priest and will enter as others could not enter into the Holy Place, a priest after the order of Melchizedek.

Calvin builds the same conclusion from the constitution of the people rather than from the words. The Jews had been so taught that they placed their whole confidence as to their salvation on the king God had set over them; the happiness and safety of the church was always founded on the king, and he being taken away it was all over with the church. Not that David was able by his own power to save the people, but because he typically personated Christ. There is now no earthly king who is the image of Christ, since Christ alone gives life to the church, but it was then set forth figuratively that the king was, as it were, the soul of the community. Calvin therefore hears in the promise something like a resurrection, for the people were in exile as dead men, their hope of public safety having vanished when their king was destroyed.

The covenant formula draws agreement. Clarke says only that the old covenant shall be renewed. Keil and Delitzsch make it the attainment of the divine calling, when Israel really becomes the people of the Lord and the salvation of Israel is complete. Gill applies it to a people long called not his people, now converted, the covenant of grace being renewed and freshly applied so that they behave as the people of God and worship him. Calvin calls the mode of speaking one we meet with everywhere in the prophets, very expressive and including the whole of true happiness, and sets beside it the saying of the Psalmist that blessed are the people whose God is Jehovah. Though nothing else were wanting that could be expected, until we feel assured that God is a Father to us and that we are his people, whatever happiness we have will only end in misery. He adds that the scattered had not been one body, and that God promises the gathering of that church from which the ten tribes had fallen off when they revolted from the family of David.
23:
The turn from promise to tempest strikes Calvin as abrupt. Nothing could be more delightful than the promise that God would be a Father to the people, and then at once a whirlwind arises which will abide on the head of the wicked; at first view the two do not harmonize. He offers two ways of joining them. The threat may be applied to the heathens, or to any of the enemies of the church, since whenever God appears as the Saviour of his people his vengeance goes forth and is poured on the wicked; Isaiah joins the favour of God and his vengeance in the same way, so that mercy toward the faithful cannot be clearly and distinctly perceived unless judgment on the wicked is made conspicuous. Or the words may be read as spoken to the people themselves: the prophet had kindly endeavoured to allure them by offering them favour, and having seen that the greater part would despise it, he seasonably threatens that such ingratitude could not be borne.

The others fix the tempest more narrowly. Clarke makes it a grievous tempest of desolation falling on Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans. Gill leaves the target general, taking it as the wrath of God, which like a whirlwind comes suddenly with great force and carries all before it, so that there is no withstanding it, and directing it against the enemies of his church and people. Wesley catches the force of the word continuing: not a sudden blast that shall presently go over, but a vengeance that shall abide. Gill reads the verse following as the explanation of that very word. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the two verses have already been met with earlier in the book with a few variations, and that one of the substitutions merely disturbs a play on words rather than destroying it, since the two consonants are kindred sounds.

Calvin compares the vengeance to a messenger or a minister who is sent to carry a message or to perform what has been commanded him, and appeals to the saying of Isaiah that the word of God shall not return void. Those who take that saying to mean only that the word brings forth fruit understand the passage wrongly, since the effect spoken of is either for salvation or for perdition. So here the vengeance, once gone forth, shall not return until it fulfils what has been commanded. The thoughts of the heart he takes for the decrees or purposes of God, granting that the expression is metaphorical and taken from men, since it is not consistent with what God is either to think or to deliberate; but the sense is not ambiguous, that when vengeance is sent forth the wicked must perish, for so it has been decreed, and the purposes of God can never be frustrated.

On the latter days the voices look forward differently. Wesley keeps the words within the experience of the hearers: though at present they will not consider, yet afterward, when they see the things come to pass, they shall consider what they were told. Clarke understands the latter days of the Gospel dispensation, and takes the restoration which is the principal topic of this chapter and the one following to belong to that time.
